chapters.title: Between the Testaments: from Exile to AD 135
chapters.subtitle: The 600 years that set the stage for Jesus
chapters.nutshell: Between the last prophets and the birth of Jesus, Israel passed from Persian to Greek to Jewish to Roman rule. These centuries gave the New Testament its world: synagogues, Pharisees, Herod's Temple, Roman soldiers and a deep hope for God's Messiah.
chapters.bigIdea: The 'silent' years between the Testaments were full of events that explain almost every page of the Gospels.
skeleton: Exile and return under Persia (586–332 BC)
Greek rule after Alexander (332–167 BC)
The Maccabees revolt and win freedom (167–63 BC)
Rome takes control and Herod rules (63–4 BC)
Jesus and the apostles live under Rome
Two failed revolts end with the Temple and Jerusalem lost (AD 66–135)

p: In 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple and took many Judeans into exile. In 539 BC Persia conquered Babylon, and King Cyrus allowed the exiles to go home (Ezra 1:1–4). They rebuilt a smaller **Second Temple**, finished about 516 BC. Ezra and Nehemiah taught the Torah and rebuilt the walls. For about two hundred years Judea was a small, quiet province of the Persian Empire.

In 332 BC **Alexander the Great** swept through the land. After his early death his generals divided the empire. Judea was ruled first by the **Ptolemies** of Egypt (about 301–198 BC) and then by the **Seleucids** of Syria. Greek language, cities, theatres and gymnasiums spread everywhere. In Alexandria, Jews translated the Torah into Greek (the **Septuagint**), the Bible the apostles often quoted.

In 167 BC the Seleucid king **Antiochus IV** banned circumcision, Sabbath and Torah reading, and set up a pagan altar in the Temple. A priest named Mattathias and his sons, led by **Judah the Maccabee** ('the hammer'), rebelled. In 164 BC they cleansed and rededicated the Temple (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). Jews still remember this as **Hanukkah**, the Feast of Dedication that Jesus attended (John 10:22).

The Maccabees' family, the **Hasmoneans**, then ruled an independent Jewish kingdom for about eighty years. But they also took the office of High Priest, and quarrels about this helped give rise to groups like the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes.

In 63 BC two Hasmonean brothers were fighting for the throne. The Roman general **Pompey** came, captured Jerusalem and even walked into the Holy of Holies. Judea now belonged to Rome. In 40 BC the Roman Senate named **Herod** 'king of the Jews', and he ruled from 37 to 4 BC. He was a brilliant builder and a cruel ruler. Jesus was born near the end of his reign (Matthew 2:1).

sections.h: Jesus, the war and the end of the Temple
p: After Herod, Rome ruled Judea through governors such as **Pontius Pilate** (AD 26–36). Anger at Roman rule grew until the **Jewish War** broke out in AD 66. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple, as Jesus had warned (Luke 19:41–44). The last rebels died at **Masada** in AD 73 or 74.

> A second revolt led by **Simon bar Kokhba** (AD 132–135) also failed. Rome rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan city called Aelia Capitolina and banned Jews from it. Judaism continued around the Torah, the synagogue and the rabbis; the church spread across the empire.

chapters.title: Background to the Gospels
chapters.subtitle: How Jesus' words became four books
chapters.nutshell: Jesus taught as a Jewish rabbi, and his disciples remembered and passed on his words. Within a few decades these memories were written down as four Gospels, each telling the one story for a different audience.
chapters.bigIdea: Four Gospels give four portraits of one Jesus, each rooted in the Jewish world.
skeleton: Jesus teaches in memorable Jewish ways
Disciples memorise and pass on his words
The Gospels are written, roughly AD 60–100
Each Gospel speaks to its own audience
Matthew, Mark and Luke are closely related; John is different
Each is deeply Jewish in its own way

sections.h: From Jesus' lips to the page
p: Jesus did not write a book. He taught in short sayings, parables and vivid pictures that were easy to remember, as Jewish teachers did. His disciples lived with him and repeated his words. Jewish students were trained to memorise their teacher's words carefully. The Mishnah begins: 'Moses **received** the Torah from Sinai and **handed it on**…' (Avot 1:1). Paul uses the same language: 'I delivered to you… what I also received' (1 Corinthians 15:3).

Luke says that many had already written accounts, based on eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). Most scholars date Mark around AD 65–70, Matthew and Luke around AD 70–90, and John around AD 90–100. Some date them earlier. These dates are **estimates**, not certainties. Either way, they were written within living memory of Jesus, when eyewitnesses were still alive.

sections.h: Who wrote them, and for whom?
p: The Gospels themselves do not name their authors, but early church tradition is strong. **Matthew** the tax collector wrote for Jewish believers. **Mark**, Peter's companion, wrote in Rome for Gentile believers. **Luke**, a doctor and Paul's companion, wrote for Theophilus and the wider Greek world. **John**, 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', wrote last, traditionally from Ephesus. Around AD 180 Irenaeus already spoke of exactly four Gospels.

Matthew, Mark and Luke share many stories, often in the same order and words. They are called the **Synoptic Gospels** ('seen together'). A widely held view is that Mark was written first and Matthew and Luke used it, along with other sources; but this is a scholarly theory, and others are proposed.
**John** is different. It tells fewer miracles, calls them 'signs', and gives long speeches of Jesus. It follows the Jewish feasts: three Passovers, Tabernacles and Hanukkah.

**Matthew** shows Jesus fulfilling the Scriptures ('this was to fulfil…') and teaching the Torah from a mountain like a new Moses. **Mark** explains Jewish customs and Aramaic words for non-Jewish readers (Mark 5:41; 7:3–4). **Luke** begins and ends in the Temple (Luke 1:8–9; 24:53) and shows God welcoming outsiders. **John** presents Jesus as the meaning of the feasts: the Passover Lamb, the living water and the light of the world.

chapters.title: The Land: Geography of Jesus' World
chapters.subtitle: Hills, lakes, deserts and roads
chapters.nutshell: Jesus' land was very small, but full of contrasts: green Galilee, rocky Judea, a freshwater lake and the salty Dead Sea. Knowing its regions, roads and people helps the Gospel stories come alive.
chapters.bigIdea: The geography of the land shapes the movements and meaning of Jesus' ministry.
skeleton: A small land between sea and desert
Many regions with different rulers and peoples
Main roads link Egypt and Syria
Jews and Samaritans avoid each other
Jesus' ministry centres on the Sea of Galilee
His last journey goes 'up' to Jerusalem

p: From Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south is only about 240 km. Yet the land changes quickly: the Mediterranean coast, the central hill country, the deep Jordan valley, and the wilderness to the east. The **Sea of Galilee** lies about 210 m below sea level, and the **Dead Sea**, about 430 m below, is the lowest place on earth. Rain falls in winter; summers are dry.

In Jesus' day the land was a patchwork. **Galilee** and **Perea** (across the Jordan) were ruled by Herod Antipas. **Judea**, **Samaria** and **Idumea** were under a Roman governor. **Gaulanitis**, north-east of the lake, belonged to Herod's son Philip. The **Decapolis** ('ten cities') was a group of Greek cities, and **Phoenicia** with Tyre and Sidon lay on the coast. Jesus visited them all (Mark 7:24, 31).

Three main routes ran north–south. The **coastal road**, later called the Via Maris ('way of the sea', compare Isaiah 9:1), linked Egypt and Syria. The **ridge route** ran along the hilltops through Shechem, Bethel, Jerusalem and Hebron, the road of the patriarchs. The **Jordan valley route** ran beside the river. Most people walked about 30 km a day, often in groups for safety (Luke 2:44; 10:30).

The Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem, and centuries of hostility divided them from Jews: 'Jews have no dealings with Samaritans' (John 4:9). Galilean pilgrims often went around Samaria through the Jordan valley, though some went straight through. Jesus did both (Luke 9:51–53; John 4:4).

Jerusalem stands about 750 m above sea level, and Jericho about 250 m below. So pilgrims really did 'go up' to Jerusalem: a climb of about 1,000 m in 25 km of desert road, the setting of the Good Samaritan story (Luke 10:30).

The **Sea of Galilee** is a freshwater lake about 21 km long. Its towns, Capernaum, Bethsaida and Magdala, lived by fishing and trade. Winds from the hills can raise sudden storms (Mark 4:37). Most of Jesus' miracles happened around this lake.
East of Jerusalem the **Judean wilderness** drops to the Dead Sea: bare hills, caves and silence. Here David hid, John the Baptist preached, and Jesus was tested for forty days (Mark 1:12–13).

chapters.title: Rome: Empire, Emperor and Everyday Power
chapters.subtitle: Who was really in charge, and how the Gospel answered
chapters.nutshell: In Jesus' day Rome ruled the whole Mediterranean world. Emperors called themselves 'son of god', 'lord' and 'saviour' and announced their 'good news'. The New Testament used these very words to proclaim that Jesus, not Caesar, is the true Lord.
chapters.bigIdea: The Gospel announced a King whose kingdom answers Rome's power with the cross and the resurrection.
skeleton: Rome ruled through emperors, governors and client kings
Taxes and toll collectors reached every village
Soldiers and crucifixion kept order by fear
Roman peace, roads and Greek helped the Gospel spread
Emperor titles were used for Jesus
Paul's Roman citizenship shaped his mission

p: **Augustus** became the first emperor in 27 BC; his census is in Luke 2:1. **Tiberius** ruled during Jesus' ministry (Luke 3:1). Rome governed through layers of power. A **client king** like Herod ruled with Rome's permission. Later Judea had a Roman **prefect**, such as **Pontius Pilate** (AD 26–36); an inscription found at Caesarea gives him this title. The governor alone could order an execution (John 18:31).

Rome demanded tribute from every province. A census in AD 6 sparked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). Besides land and head taxes, there were tolls on goods at roads and harbours. Local men bought the right to collect them and took extra for themselves, so **tax collectors** were hated as greedy collaborators. Yet Jesus called Matthew (Matthew 9:9) and ate with Zacchaeus (Luke 19:1–10).
When asked about tribute, Jesus held up a denarius with Caesar's image: 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17).

Roman soldiers were everywhere. A **centurion** commanded about eighty men. Some centurions in the Gospels and Acts showed great faith (Matthew 8:5–13; Acts 10). **Crucifixion** was Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels: public, slow and shameful, a warning to everyone passing by. The Roman orator Cicero called it 'the most cruel and terrible punishment'. Roman citizens were normally spared it.
> That Jesus died this death, and that a centurion said, 'Truly this man was the Son of God' (Mark 15:39), was a shock to the whole Roman world.

The **Pax Romana** (Roman peace) meant fewer wars between nations, though it was kept by force. Roman roads and safe sea routes linked the cities of the empire. Across the East, ordinary people spoke **common Greek** (koinē). This is why the New Testament was written in Greek, and why Paul could travel and preach from Jerusalem to Rome.

Emperors were honoured with grand titles. Augustus was called 'son of god' (son of the deified Julius Caesar), 'saviour' and 'lord'. An inscription from Priene (9 BC) called his birthday the beginning of 'good news' (euangelia) for the world. The apostles used the same words for Jesus: 'good news… a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord' (Luke 2:10–11). Confessing 'Jesus is Lord' (Romans 10:9) meant Caesar was not the ultimate lord (Acts 17:7).

Paul was born a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25–29). Citizens could not be beaten without trial and could appeal to the emperor. Paul used these rights to protect the young church (Acts 16:37) and to bring the Gospel to Rome itself (Acts 25:11). He was proud of his citizenship, yet wrote that 'our citizenship is in heaven' (Philippians 3:20).
